note: Biology round 3: four data passages (quadrat, food tests, germination, potometer) and applied items across the JAMB syllabus.

passages.title: Quadrat study of a school field
passages.text:
A student threw a 1 m² quadrat at random
ten times on a school field of area 500 m²
and recorded the number of each plant
species inside the quadrat at every throw.
The totals for the ten throws are shown
below.

Species              Total count
Elephant grass           120
Sida (broom weed)         60
Tridax                    40
Goat weed                 20

passages.title: Food tests on four samples
passages.text:
Four food samples, W, X, Y and Z, were
tested in the laboratory. The results are
shown below (+ means a positive result, -
means negative).

Test                  W    X    Y    Z
Iodine solution       +    -    -    +
Benedict's solution   -    +    -    -
Biuret test           -    +    +    +
Sudan III             -    +    +    -

passages.title: Germination of bean seeds
passages.text:
Five test tubes, each containing five bean
seeds on cotton wool, were kept for one
week under the conditions described below.
In tube E the seeds were covered with
boiled, cooled water and a layer of oil.

Tube   Conditions              Result
A      moist, warm, light      all grew
B      moist, warm, dark       all grew
C      dry, warm, light        none
D      moist, in a fridge      none
E      moist, warm, no air     none

passages.title: Transpiration measured with a potometer
passages.text:
A leafy shoot was set up in a potometer
and the distance moved by the air bubble
in ten minutes was recorded under four
different conditions.

Condition                 Distance (mm)
Still air, shade               12
Still air, sunlight            30
Fan blowing, sunlight          55
Leaves coated with
  vaseline, sunlight            4

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: From the quadrat data above, the estimated population of Tridax on the whole field is
questions.explanation: Density = 40 plants in 10 m² = 4 per m²; population = 4 × 500 m² = 2,000 plants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: From the quadrat data above, the species with the highest population density is
questions.explanation: Elephant grass had 120 plants in 10 m² (12 per m²), the highest count of the four species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the quadrat study above, the quadrat was thrown at random in order to
questions.D: avoid bias in choosing the sample areas
questions.explanation: Random sampling ensures every part of the field has an equal chance of being sampled, so the estimate is not biased.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: From the quadrat data above, the total density of all plants on the field is
questions.explanation: Total plants counted = 120 + 60 + 40 + 20 = 240 in ten 1 m² quadrats, i.e. 24 plants per m².

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The quadrat method used in the study above would be least suitable for estimating the population of
questions.A: grasses growing on a school lawn
questions.B: weeds growing between rows on a farm
questions.C: snails crawling on the field at night
questions.D: birds nesting in the trees round the field
questions.explanation: Quadrats suit plants and slow-moving or sessile animals; birds move too fast and too far to be counted in a fixed frame.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: From the food-test results above, the sample that contains starch only is
questions.explanation: W gives a positive iodine test (starch) and is negative for the other three tests. Z also contains starch, but its positive Biuret test shows that it contains protein as well.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: From the food-test results above, sample Y is most likely
questions.explanation: Y is positive for protein (Biuret) and fat (Sudan III); groundnuts are rich in both protein and oil.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: From the food-test results above, sample X could be
questions.explanation: X contains reducing sugar (lactose), protein and fat, the three food classes found in milk; Y has no sugar, so it is not milk.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the food tests above, a positive Biuret test is shown by a colour change to
questions.explanation: Biuret reagent turns purple/violet with proteins; blue-black is iodine with starch and brick red is Benedict's with reducing sugar.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the food tests above, before the Benedict's result for X could be read, the mixture of X and Benedict's solution had to be
questions.explanation: Benedict's test only works when the food and reagent are heated; a brick-red precipitate then shows reducing sugar.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the germination experiment above, a comparison of tubes A and B shows that
questions.A: light is not necessary for germination
questions.C: warmth is not necessary for germination
questions.D: seeds germinate faster in the dark
questions.explanation: A and B differ only in light, yet both sets germinated, so light is not a requirement for germination.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the germination experiment above, tubes A and C together show that germination requires
questions.explanation: A and C differ only in moisture; the dry seeds in C did not germinate, so water is necessary.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the germination experiment above, the seeds in tube D failed to germinate because
questions.A: the cold in the fridge killed the seed embryos
questions.B: the inside of the fridge was completely dark
questions.C: there was far too much water in the tube
questions.D: low temperature stopped the enzymes from working
questions.explanation: Germination depends on enzymes that break down stored food; near 4 °C they are practically inactive. B shows darkness alone does not prevent germination.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the germination experiment above, the boiled, cooled water and oil layer in tube E were used to
questions.explanation: Boiling drives dissolved air out of water and the oil layer stops air re-entering, so tube E tests the need for oxygen.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The bean seeds in the experiment above show epigeal germination, which means that
questions.A: the cotyledons are carried above the soil
questions.B: the cotyledons remain below the soil
questions.explanation: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above ground, as in beans; maize shows hypogeal germination.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The potometer in the experiment above directly measures the rate of
questions.explanation: A potometer measures how fast the cut shoot draws in water; this is taken as roughly equal to the rate of transpiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: From the potometer data above, the rate of transpiration in sunlight was how many times the rate in shade (still air)?
questions.explanation: Sunlight, still air: 30 mm; shade, still air: 12 mm; 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 times.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the potometer experiment above, the fan increased the distance moved by the bubble because moving air
questions.A: cools the leaves and closes the stomata
questions.B: increases the pressure in the xylem
questions.D: removes water vapour from around the leaves
questions.explanation: Wind blows away the humid layer round the leaf, steepening the diffusion gradient for water vapour, so transpiration rises.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the potometer experiment above, coating the leaves with vaseline reduced the reading because the vaseline
questions.explanation: Vaseline seals the stomatal pores through which most water vapour escapes, so very little water was drawn up.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In setting up the potometer above, the shoot was cut and fitted under water in order to
questions.A: wash off dust from the leaves
questions.B: supply mineral salts to the shoot
questions.D: prevent air bubbles from entering the xylem
questions.explanation: An air lock in the xylem would break the water column and stop uptake, so the cut end must never be exposed to air.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Viruses are described as being on the borderline between living and non-living things because they
questions.A: have cells with cytoplasm but no true nuclei
questions.B: move about freely in air, water and soil like bacteria
questions.C: feed, grow and respire in the same way as bacteria
questions.D: multiply only inside living cells but can be crystallised
questions.explanation: Outside a host a virus is an inert particle that can even form crystals; inside a living cell it multiplies, so it shows life only when parasitising a cell.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: An organism consists of a single cell with no membrane-bound nucleus and a cell wall that is not made of cellulose. It belongs to the kingdom
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic cells (no true nucleus) with non-cellulose walls are characteristic of bacteria and blue-green algae, kingdom Monera.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Euglena is difficult to place among plants or animals because it
questions.A: has a cellulose cell wall as well as a whip-like flagellum
questions.B: lacks both a nucleus and chloroplasts like a bacterium
questions.C: reproduces by spores in the same way as a fungus does
questions.D: has chloroplasts yet swims with a flagellum and can feed like an animal
questions.explanation: Euglena photosynthesises like a plant but moves with a flagellum, has no cellulose wall and can feed heterotrophically in the dark, like an animal.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Rhizopus (bread mould) is classified as a fungus rather than a plant because it
questions.A: grows on stale bread and other cooked foods
questions.B: has true roots, stems and leaves like a plant
questions.C: produces flowers and seeds like a plant
questions.D: lacks chlorophyll and feeds saprophytically through hyphae
questions.explanation: Fungi have no chlorophyll, so they absorb digested food from dead matter through thread-like hyphae; their walls contain chitin, not cellulose.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Mosses are usually found in damp, shady places mainly because
questions.A: they cannot tolerate direct sunlight for long
questions.B: their spores can only be dispersed by water
questions.C: they feed on the decaying leaves found there
questions.D: their male gametes must swim in water to reach the eggs
questions.explanation: Bryophytes have no vascular tissue and their sperms need a film of water to swim to the archegonia, so they depend on moisture.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A fern differs from a moss in that the fern
questions.A: reproduces by means of seeds instead of spores
questions.B: shows no alternation of generations in its life
questions.C: needs no water at all for fertilisation to occur
questions.D: has true roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue
questions.explanation: Ferns (Pteridophyta) are vascular plants with true roots, stems and fronds; spores develop in sori under the fronds. Mosses lack vascular tissue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A student finds an animal with a soft unsegmented body, a muscular foot and a coiled shell. It belongs to the phylum
questions.explanation: A muscular foot, mantle and (usually) a calcareous shell are the diagnostic features of molluscs such as snails.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: An animal has two body divisions, four pairs of walking legs and no antennae. It is
questions.explanation: Arachnids (spiders, scorpions, ticks) have cephalothorax and abdomen, eight legs and no antennae; insects have three body parts, six legs and one pair of antennae.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A student examines an animal with a dry scaly skin that lays eggs with leathery shells on land. It belongs to the class
questions.explanation: Reptiles such as lizards and snakes have dry scaly skins and lay leathery-shelled eggs on land; amphibians have moist skins and breed in water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Birds and mammals resemble each other in that both
questions.A: maintain a constant body temperature and have a four-chambered heart
questions.B: have feathers on their bodies and lay eggs with hard shells
questions.C: have hair on their bodies and feed their young on milk
questions.D: possess a muscular diaphragm and light hollow bones
questions.explanation: Both classes are homoiothermic (warm-blooded) with a completely divided four-chambered heart; feathers are for birds only and hair for mammals only.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Which feature of the tapeworm is an adaptation to living in the intestine of its host?
questions.C: a thick cuticle that resists digestive enzymes
questions.explanation: The tapeworm has no gut; it absorbs digested food through its body surface, holds on with hooks and suckers and is protected by a cuticle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The clitellum of the earthworm functions in
questions.A: locomotion through the burrows in the soil
questions.B: sensing light and touch at the front end
questions.C: gaseous exchange through the moist body wall
questions.D: secreting the cocoon in which fertilised eggs are laid
questions.explanation: The swollen clitellum secretes mucus and the cocoon; the earthworm is hermaphrodite but cross-fertilises.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Hydra captures and paralyses its prey by means of
questions.explanation: The tentacles carry nematocysts (stinging cells) that discharge threads to paralyse small animals, which are then pushed into the mouth.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The lateral line of a bony fish enables it to
questions.A: see clearly in dim light at the bottom of the river
questions.B: regulate its body temperature in cold water
questions.C: detect vibrations and pressure changes in the water
questions.D: control its buoyancy at different depths
questions.explanation: The lateral line is a row of sensory pits that detect water movement; buoyancy is controlled by the swim bladder.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Pine and cycads are classified as gymnosperms because their
questions.A: seeds are borne naked on cone scales
questions.explanation: Gymnosperm means naked seed: the ovules lie exposed on the scales of cones instead of inside an ovary.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A plant has leaves with parallel veins, a fibrous root system and floral parts in threes. It is
questions.explanation: Parallel venation, fibrous roots, floral parts in threes and one cotyledon are the marks of monocots such as maize and grasses.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A cell has a biconcave shape, contains haemoglobin and lacks a nucleus. Which of the following statements about it is correct?
questions.A: It transports oxygen from the lungs to the tissues
questions.B: It engulfs bacteria that enter the body
questions.C: It helps the blood to clot at a wound
questions.explanation: The biconcave, nucleus-free cell packed with haemoglobin is a red blood cell, whose job is to carry oxygen; white cells engulf germs and make antibodies, platelets clot blood.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Which organelle would be most abundant in the flight muscle cells of a bird?
questions.explanation: Flight demands a great deal of energy, which is released in the mitochondria during aerobic respiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Proteins are assembled in the cell on the
questions.explanation: Ribosomes, free or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum, are the sites of protein synthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Red blood cells placed in distilled water swell and burst, but onion cells in distilled water do not, because onion cells
questions.D: are surrounded by a rigid cellulose wall
questions.explanation: Water enters both by osmosis; the plant cell wall resists further expansion and the cell merely becomes turgid, while the animal cell haemolyses.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A strip of yam placed in a concentrated salt solution for an hour becomes soft and limp because its cells
questions.A: lose water by osmosis and become flaccid
questions.B: gain water by osmosis and finally burst
questions.C: absorb the salt rapidly by diffusion
questions.D: die quickly from a lack of oxygen
questions.explanation: Water moves out of the cells into the stronger solution; the protoplasts shrink (plasmolysis) and the tissue loses turgor.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Root hair cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water even when the concentration inside the cell is already higher than outside. The process involved is
questions.explanation: Movement against a concentration gradient needs energy from respiration, which is active transport; that is why roots need oxygen.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The spreading of the smell of perfume across a room illustrates
questions.explanation: Perfume molecules move from a region of high concentration to regions of low concentration until evenly spread: diffusion.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The level of organisation shown by Hydra, whose body has distinct layers of similar cells working together, is
questions.explanation: Hydra's two cell layers act as tissues but it has no true organs; Amoeba is at cell level, flatworms at organ level and earthworms at system level.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Which of the following statements is NOT part of the cell theory?
questions.A: All living things are made up of cells
questions.B: New cells arise from pre-existing cells
questions.D: The cell is the basic unit of life
questions.explanation: Only photosynthetic plant cells contain chloroplasts; the cell theory makes no such claim.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A cell from which the nucleus has been removed soon dies because the nucleus
questions.A: controls the activities of the cell and carries the chromosomes
questions.B: stores the food reserves on which the cell feeds
questions.C: releases all the energy the cell needs for its work
questions.D: makes the cell wall and the cell membrane
questions.explanation: The nucleus carries the genetic material that directs protein synthesis and cell division; without it the cell cannot maintain itself.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In testing a leaf for starch, the leaf is boiled in alcohol in order to
questions.A: kill the leaf and stop all its chemical reactions
questions.B: soften the waxy cuticle so that iodine can enter
questions.C: remove the chlorophyll so that the iodine colour can be seen
questions.D: dissolve the starch so that it can be tested
questions.explanation: The leaf is first boiled in water to kill it and burst the cells, then in alcohol to decolourise it; iodine then shows starch as blue-black.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A potted plant is kept in a dark cupboard for 48 hours before an experiment on photosynthesis in order to
questions.D: remove starch already stored in the leaves
questions.explanation: Destarching ensures that any starch found after the experiment was made during the experiment itself.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A destarched potted plant had one leaf enclosed in a flask containing soda lime (which absorbs carbon dioxide) and was left in sunlight for six hours. When tested with iodine the enclosed leaf stayed brown while an uncovered leaf turned blue-black. This shows that photosynthesis requires
questions.explanation: The enclosed leaf had light and chlorophyll but no carbon dioxide (removed by the soda lime), so it made no starch; the uncovered leaf did.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A farmer notices that his maize plants are stunted and their older leaves have turned pale yellow. The soil is most likely deficient in
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is needed for proteins and chlorophyll; deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing (chlorosis) that begins in the older leaves.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Magnesium is an essential mineral element for green plants because it is a component of
questions.explanation: Each chlorophyll molecule has a magnesium atom at its centre, so magnesium shortage causes chlorosis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Insectivorous plants such as the pitcher plant and sundew trap insects because they usually grow in soils that are poor in
questions.explanation: The digested insects supply nitrogenous compounds that the waterlogged, acidic soils cannot provide; the plants still photosynthesise.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A patient whose bile duct is blocked would have the greatest difficulty in digesting
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify fats into tiny droplets so that lipase can act; without bile most fat passes out undigested.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The hydrochloric acid in gastric juice
questions.A: digests proteins directly into amino acids
questions.B: emulsifies fats into tiny droplets for lipase
questions.C: gives pepsin the acid medium it needs and kills germs in food
questions.D: neutralises the alkaline juice from the pancreas
questions.explanation: Pepsin works best at about pH 2; the acid also destroys many microbes swallowed with food.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The ileum is well adapted for absorbing digested food because it
questions.A: has thick muscular walls that churn the food
questions.B: is the shortest and widest part of the gut
questions.C: secretes hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin
questions.D: has numerous villi with thin walls and a rich blood supply
questions.explanation: Villi and microvilli give a huge surface area; each villus has capillaries for sugars and amino acids and a lacteal for fats.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Saliva that has been boiled is mixed with starch solution and kept at 37 °C for 30 minutes. Iodine still turns the mixture blue-black because
questions.A: boiling destroyed the amylase in the saliva
questions.B: starch cannot be digested by saliva
questions.C: 37 °C is too cold for the enzyme
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins that are permanently denatured by boiling; unboiled saliva at 37 °C would have converted the starch to maltose.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The dental formula of an adult human is I 2/2, C 1/1, Pm 2/2, M 3/3. The total number of teeth is
questions.explanation: The formula gives one half of the upper and lower jaws: (2 + 1 + 2 + 3) × 2 = 16 per jaw, 32 teeth altogether.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The diastema (a gap without teeth) in the jaw of a goat allows
questions.A: the tongue to hold cut grass aside while other grass is being chewed
questions.B: the animal to bite off grass close to the ground
questions.C: the canines to grow longer without damaging the lips
questions.D: the animal to breathe freely while it is eating
questions.explanation: Herbivores have no upper incisors or canines; the gap lets the tongue separate cut grass from the grass being ground by the molars.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A sailor who has eaten no fresh fruit or vegetables for months develops swollen, bleeding gums and wounds that refuse to heal. He is suffering from
questions.explanation: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C (ascorbic acid), found in fresh fruit and vegetables; it causes bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A food sample rubbed on filter paper leaves a permanent translucent mark. The sample contains
questions.explanation: The grease-spot test: fats and oils leave a translucent patch that does not dry off, unlike water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Which of the following organisms is a saprophyte?
questions.B: a lion feeding on an antelope
questions.C: a mistletoe on a mango tree
questions.D: a mushroom growing on a dead log
questions.explanation: Saprophytes feed on dead organic matter; the tapeworm and mistletoe are parasites and the lion is a holozoic carnivore.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The pulmonary artery differs from all other arteries in that it carries
questions.explanation: It carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs; the pulmonary vein is the only vein that carries oxygenated blood.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A complete ring of bark was removed from a woody stem. After some weeks the bark just above the ring swelled. This shows that
questions.A: water moves down the stem in the xylem
questions.B: the stem was infected by fungi
questions.C: manufactured food moves down the stem in the phloem
questions.D: the xylem lies in the bark
questions.explanation: Removing the bark removes the phloem; sugars moving down from the leaves accumulate above the ring, causing the swelling.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A well-watered plant wilts on a hot, dry afternoon and recovers in the evening because during the afternoon
questions.A: the roots stop absorbing water from the hot soil
questions.B: the stomata are tightly closed by the heat
questions.C: photosynthesis uses up all the water in the leaves
questions.D: water is lost by transpiration faster than it is absorbed
questions.explanation: Rapid transpiration makes cells lose turgor temporarily; in the cool evening absorption catches up and turgor is restored.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The main force that pulls water to the top of a tall tree is
questions.explanation: Evaporation from the leaves creates a suction transmitted down the continuous water columns in the xylem (cohesion-tension).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A person of blood group O can donate blood to people of all ABO groups because the red cells of group O
questions.A: have both antigens A and B
questions.C: have neither antigen A nor antigen B
questions.explanation: Without A or B antigens on the cells, the recipient's antibodies have nothing to clump; group AB people are universal recipients.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Veins possess valves but arteries do not, because in veins the blood
questions.A: flows much faster than in the arteries
questions.B: contains far more red cells and platelets
questions.C: is always oxygenated and bright red
questions.D: is under low pressure and could flow backwards
questions.explanation: Valves prevent backflow in the low-pressure return to the heart; skeletal muscles squeezing the veins help push the blood along.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right ventricle because the left ventricle
questions.A: pumps blood round the whole body
questions.explanation: The left ventricle must generate enough pressure to drive blood through the systemic circulation; the right pumps only to the nearby lungs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A person who bleeds for an unusually long time from small cuts probably has a shortage of
questions.explanation: Platelets start the clotting process that seals a wound; their deficiency prolongs bleeding.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Lymph differs from blood in that lymph
questions.explanation: Lymph is tissue fluid drained into lymph vessels; it carries lymphocytes and absorbed fats but no red cells or platelets.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: People who live at high altitudes have more red blood cells than those at sea level because at high altitudes
questions.A: the air is much colder all the year
questions.B: there is much more sunlight there
questions.C: food is scarce in the mountains
questions.D: the air contains less oxygen per breath
questions.explanation: With less oxygen available, the body makes more red cells and haemoglobin to carry enough oxygen to the tissues.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Transpiration from a leaf would be fastest on a day that is
questions.explanation: Heat and dryness increase evaporation, and wind carries the vapour away, keeping the diffusion gradient steep.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Germinating bean seeds were placed in one vacuum flask and boiled seeds in another, each with a thermometer. After two days the temperature in the first flask had risen by several degrees. This shows that germinating seeds
questions.explanation: Some of the energy released in respiration is lost as heat; the boiled (dead) seeds in the control flask do not respire, so their flask stays at room temperature.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Bread dough rises when it is left in a warm place after yeast has been added because the yeast
questions.A: absorbs water from the flour and swells up
questions.B: produces heat that expands the dough
questions.C: releases carbon dioxide by fermenting the sugars in the flour
questions.D: breaks down the gluten into gases
questions.explanation: Yeast respires anaerobically (fermentation), converting sugars to ethanol and carbon dioxide; the trapped gas bubbles make the dough rise.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The cramps and fatigue felt in the muscles after vigorous exercise are due to the accumulation of
questions.explanation: When oxygen supply cannot keep up, muscles respire anaerobically, forming lactic acid; the oxygen debt is repaid afterwards by rapid breathing.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: During inspiration (breathing in) in humans,
questions.A: the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the ribs move up and out
questions.C: the volume of the chest decreases
questions.D: the pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric
questions.explanation: These movements enlarge the thorax, lowering the pressure in the lungs so that air flows in.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Insects exchange gases with the air through
questions.A: gills on the sides of the abdomen
questions.B: the moist surface of the whole body
questions.C: spiracles leading into a system of tracheae
questions.D: a pair of lungs inside the thorax
questions.explanation: Air enters through spiracles and travels along tracheae and tracheoles directly to the tissues, so insect blood carries little oxygen.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Aerobic respiration is more useful to an organism than anaerobic respiration because aerobic respiration
questions.A: needs no enzymes to break down the glucose
questions.B: occurs only in green plants during the day
questions.C: produces alcohol that the organism can use
questions.D: releases far more energy from each molecule of glucose
questions.explanation: Complete oxidation of glucose to carbon dioxide and water yields about 38 ATP, compared with 2 ATP from anaerobic breakdown.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The gill filaments of a fish are numerous, thin and richly supplied with blood in order to
questions.A: increase the surface area for gas exchange
questions.B: filter food particles from the water
questions.C: help the fish to swim faster in water
questions.D: store oxygen for use when water is short
questions.explanation: A large, thin, well-perfused surface allows rapid diffusion of oxygen from water into the blood.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A green plant kept in complete darkness for 24 hours will
questions.C: release carbon dioxide and use up stored food
questions.explanation: In the dark photosynthesis stops but respiration continues, so the plant gives out carbon dioxide and its starch reserves fall.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Hydrogen carbonate indicator turns yellow when a small animal is kept in a sealed tube with it because the animal
questions.A: uses up all the oxygen in the sealed tube
questions.B: releases water vapour into the tube
questions.C: warms the solution with its body heat
questions.D: releases carbon dioxide, making the solution more acidic
questions.explanation: The indicator is red in normal air and turns yellow as dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid; it turns purple when carbon dioxide is removed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A routine test shows glucose in a patient's urine. The patient most likely suffers from
questions.explanation: Without enough insulin, blood glucose rises so high that the kidney tubules cannot reabsorb all of it and glucose appears in urine.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A student drinks two litres of water within a short time. About an hour later he passes a large volume of pale urine because
questions.A: less ADH is secreted, so the kidney tubules reabsorb less water
questions.B: more ADH is secreted, so the tubules reabsorb more water
questions.C: the extra water is excreted through the lungs
questions.D: the bladder muscles contract more strongly
questions.explanation: When the blood is diluted the pituitary releases less antidiuretic hormone, the collecting ducts reabsorb less water and a large volume of dilute urine is formed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Ultrafiltration of blood in the kidney takes place in the
questions.A: loop of Henle and the medulla
questions.explanation: High pressure in the glomerular capillaries forces water, salts, glucose and urea into the Bowman's capsule; cells and proteins stay in the blood.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A patient with severe liver disease has an abnormally low level of urea in the blood. This is because the liver is the organ that
questions.A: filters urea out of the blood
questions.B: removes urea from the body in the bile
questions.C: stores urea until it is passed in the urine
questions.D: converts excess amino acids to urea by deamination
questions.explanation: Deamination in the liver removes the amino group from surplus amino acids; the ammonia formed is converted to the less toxic urea, so a damaged liver makes less urea.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Which of the following is a way in which plants get rid of waste products?
questions.A: storing wastes such as tannins in leaves and bark that are later shed
questions.B: sweating out waste water through pores in the leaves
questions.C: passing liquid wastes out through the root hairs
questions.D: coughing waste gases out through the lenticels
questions.explanation: Plants have no excretory organs; they store wastes in tissues that are shed (leaves, bark, fruits) or exude gums, latex and resins.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The excretory products removed by the lungs are
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide and some water from respiration leave the body in exhaled air.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Protein found in a person's urine suggests damage to the
questions.explanation: Healthy glomerular walls hold back large protein molecules; when they are damaged, proteins leak into the filtrate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Glucose filtered into the kidney tubule is normally returned to the blood by
questions.A: selective reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule
questions.B: simple diffusion in the collecting duct
questions.C: osmosis in the descending loop of Henle
questions.D: active secretion in the Bowman's capsule
questions.explanation: All the useful glucose is actively reabsorbed in the first coiled tubule, so normal urine contains none.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The earthworm moves through the soil by means of
questions.A: pairs of jointed legs on each segment of the body
questions.B: a muscular foot that glides on a trail of slime
questions.C: a hydrostatic skeleton worked by muscles, with chaetae for grip
questions.D: fins and a tail that beat from side to side
questions.explanation: Fluid in the body cavity is squeezed by the muscles so that segments alternately lengthen and shorten, while bristles (chaetae) anchor the body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Insects and other arthropods must moult periodically because their
questions.A: muscles grow too fast for the body
questions.B: legs are lost and need replacing
questions.C: wings wear out and must be replaced
questions.D: exoskeleton cannot stretch as the animal grows
questions.explanation: The rigid chitinous exoskeleton is shed (ecdysis) and a new, larger one hardens; growth occurs in the short soft period between.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: When the forearm is bent at the elbow,
questions.A: the biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes
questions.B: both the biceps and triceps contract
questions.C: the triceps contracts while the biceps relaxes
questions.explanation: Biceps and triceps are antagonistic: the biceps flexes the arm and the triceps straightens it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A muscle is attached to a bone by a
questions.explanation: Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone at joints.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The vertebra that bears the odontoid process and allows the head to turn from side to side is the
questions.explanation: The axis (second cervical vertebra) has a peg on which the atlas rotates; nodding occurs between the skull and the atlas.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The type of joint at the shoulder and hip, which allows movement in all directions, is a
questions.explanation: The rounded head of the humerus or femur fits into a cup-shaped socket; elbows and knees are hinge joints.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A young herbaceous plant droops when it is short of water because
questions.explanation: Non-woody plants are held erect by the turgor pressure of their cells; when water is lost the cells become flaccid and the plant wilts.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A seedling placed near a window bends towards the light because
questions.A: light destroys auxin on the lit side, so cells there grow faster
questions.C: auxin accumulates on the shaded side, making cells there elongate more
questions.D: the roots pull the shoot towards the window
questions.explanation: Auxin moves away from light to the shaded side, where it stimulates cell elongation, so the shoot curves towards the light (positive phototropism).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The folding of the leaves of Mimosa pudica when touched is described as a nastic movement rather than a tropism because
questions.A: it takes place very slowly over several hours
questions.B: it happens only at night when there is no light
questions.C: it involves permanent growth of the leaf cells
questions.D: the response is the same whichever direction the stimulus comes from
questions.explanation: Tropisms are growth movements towards or away from a stimulus; nastic responses are the same whichever side is touched.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In a bony fish, forward propulsion is produced mainly by the
questions.A: caudal (tail) fin and the body muscles
questions.C: single dorsal fin on the back
questions.D: swim bladder in the body cavity
questions.explanation: Side-to-side beats of the tail drive the fish forward; paired fins steer and brake, and the dorsal fin prevents rolling.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A flower has large brightly coloured petals, a sweet scent, nectar at the base of the petals and sticky, spiny pollen grains. Its stigma is most likely to be
questions.A: large and feathery, hanging outside the flower
questions.B: absent, since the flower is self-pollinated
questions.C: small and sticky, held inside the flower
questions.D: long and dry, exposed to the wind
questions.explanation: These are the features of an insect-pollinated flower; its stigma is small and sticky and lies inside the flower where visiting insects brush against it, unlike the feathery exposed stigmas of wind-pollinated flowers.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Cross-pollination is more advantageous to a species than self-pollination because it
questions.A: requires much less pollen to succeed
questions.B: needs no insect or wind to carry the pollen
questions.C: is far more certain to occur every season
questions.D: produces offspring with greater variation and vigour
questions.explanation: Mixing genes from two parents increases variation, which helps the species adapt; self-pollination gives more uniform offspring.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In flowering plants, the endosperm is triploid because it is formed when
questions.A: one male nucleus fuses with the two polar nuclei of the embryo sac
questions.B: the egg cell fuses with two male nuclei at the same time
questions.C: two egg cells in the embryo sac fuse together
questions.D: the zygote divides three times without meiosis
questions.explanation: Double fertilisation: one male nucleus fertilises the egg (diploid zygote) and the other joins the two polar nuclei (triploid endosperm).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: After fertilisation in a flowering plant, the ovule develops into the
questions.explanation: The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary wall becomes the fruit (pericarp).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The edible part of the cashew is a swollen pedicel (flower stalk). The cashew is therefore described as
questions.explanation: A false fruit develops partly from tissues other than the ovary; the true fruit of the cashew is the kidney-shaped nut.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The mango fruit is classified as a drupe because it
questions.A: has a fleshy mesocarp and a hard stony endocarp round the seed
questions.B: splits open along two seams when it is ripe
questions.C: develops from many separate ovaries of one flower
questions.D: has a dry papery wall and many small seeds
questions.explanation: Drupes (mango, coconut) have a stony inner wall; berries such as tomato have soft inner walls and many seeds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The fruits of Tridax have a ring of fine hairs (pappus). This adapts them for dispersal by
questions.explanation: The hairs act like a parachute so the light fruit is carried away by air currents.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Fruits of Desmodium have hooks on their surface, an adaptation for dispersal by
questions.explanation: Hooked fruits cling to the fur of animals or clothing of people and are carried far from the parent plant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the
questions.explanation: Sperms meet the egg in the upper oviduct; the zygote then travels to the uterus, where it implants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The testes of a man are held in the scrotum outside the body cavity because
questions.A: there is not enough room for them inside the abdomen
questions.B: the scrotum protects them from injury during sport
questions.C: sperms form best at a temperature slightly below body temperature
questions.D: developing sperms need daylight to mature properly
questions.explanation: Sperm formation is impaired at 37 °C; the scrotum keeps the testes about 2-3 °C cooler.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, ovulation usually occurs on about the
questions.explanation: The egg is released about the middle of the cycle; if it is not fertilised, the uterine lining is shed about 14 days later.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The placenta of a mammal
questions.A: allows the blood of the mother and the foetus to mix freely
questions.B: stores the food that the baby will need after birth
questions.C: produces the eggs that are fertilised in the uterus
questions.D: exchanges food, oxygen and wastes without mixing the two bloods
questions.explanation: Exchange occurs by diffusion across the placental villi; the two circulations remain separate, protecting the foetus from the mother's blood pressure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Identical twins are produced when
questions.A: one fertilised egg divides into two separate embryos
questions.B: two eggs are fertilised by two sperms
questions.C: an egg is fertilised by two sperms
questions.D: two eggs are fertilised by one sperm
questions.explanation: Identical twins share all their genes because they come from one zygote; fraternal twins come from two separately fertilised eggs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Ginger is propagated vegetatively by means of
questions.explanation: The ginger 'root' is an underground stem (rhizome) with buds that sprout into new plants; cassava is grown from stem cuttings.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The life cycle of the mosquito (egg, larva, pupa, adult) is an example of
questions.explanation: Complete metamorphosis has a pupal stage; the cockroach and grasshopper show incomplete metamorphosis (egg, nymph, adult).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Yeast reproduces asexually by
questions.explanation: A small outgrowth forms on the parent cell, receives a nucleus and pinches off; Amoeba divides by binary fission.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In maize, the cotyledon remains below the ground during germination because the part of the embryo that elongates is the
questions.explanation: Hypogeal germination: the epicotyl elongates and pushes the plumule up while the cotyledon stays buried; in beans the hypocotyl elongates (epigeal).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Ink marks were made at equal intervals along a young root. After two days the marks just behind the tip had spread furthest apart. This shows that the region of greatest growth in length is
questions.A: the root cap at the very tip of the root
questions.B: the base of the root near the stem
questions.C: the region covered with root hairs
questions.D: the region of elongation just behind the tip
questions.explanation: Cells are produced at the meristem in the tip and then elongate in the zone behind it; older regions have stopped growing.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Increase in the girth of a woody stem (secondary growth) results from the activity of the
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium divides to produce new xylem inside and phloem outside, thickening the stem year by year.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Meiosis differs from mitosis in that meiosis
questions.A: produces two cells identical to the parent
questions.B: occurs in all the body cells during growth
questions.C: halves the chromosome number and produces four cells
questions.D: does not involve the chromosomes at all
questions.explanation: Meiosis occurs in the gonads (and in anthers and ovules) to form gametes with half the chromosome number; mitosis gives identical diploid cells for growth.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes. The number of chromosomes in a human sperm is
questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid, formed by meiosis, so a sperm carries 23 chromosomes; fertilisation restores 46.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Some hard-coated seeds germinate only after the coat has been scratched or partly burnt. This treatment breaks dormancy by
questions.D: allowing water and oxygen to reach the embryo
questions.explanation: The impermeable testa keeps water and air out; scarification lets them in so that germination can start.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Unripe bananas ripen faster when kept in a closed bag with a ripe one because the ripe fruit releases
questions.explanation: Ethene is a gaseous plant hormone that promotes fruit ripening; it accumulates in the closed bag.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The most reliable measure of the growth of a plant over several weeks is its increase in
questions.explanation: Dry mass excludes the water content, which varies from hour to hour, and reflects the real increase in living material.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: When a person touches a hot object and withdraws the hand before feeling pain, the impulse travels in the order
questions.A: receptor → motor neurone → brain → sensory neurone → muscle
questions.C: muscle → sensory neurone → spinal cord → receptor
questions.D: receptor → sensory neurone → spinal cord → motor neurone → muscle
questions.explanation: A spinal reflex arc passes through the spinal cord, not the brain, which is why the response is so fast; pain is felt slightly later.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A patient who staggers and cannot coordinate his movements after an accident has probably damaged the
questions.explanation: The cerebellum controls balance, posture and the coordination of voluntary movements.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Breathing and heartbeat are controlled by the
questions.explanation: The medulla at the base of the brain regulates involuntary activities such as breathing, heart rate and swallowing.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: When the eye focuses on a near object,
questions.A: the ciliary muscles relax, the ligaments tighten and the lens thins
questions.B: the pupil closes almost completely to cut out stray light
questions.C: the ciliary muscles contract, the ligaments slacken and the lens thickens
questions.D: the retina moves forward until the image is sharp
questions.explanation: A thicker, more convex lens bends light more strongly, bringing rays from a near object to a focus on the retina (accommodation).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A student can read a book clearly but cannot see the board from the back of the class. His defect and its correction are
questions.explanation: In short sight (myopia) the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens moves it back.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In dim light we see objects only in shades of grey because
questions.A: only the rods, which are insensitive to colour, respond to weak light
questions.B: the pupil closes and lets very little light in
questions.C: the cones are temporarily damaged by the lack of light
questions.D: the lens becomes cloudy and opaque in weak light
questions.explanation: Rods work in low light but cannot distinguish colours; cones give colour vision but need bright light.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The part of the ear responsible for maintaining balance is the
questions.explanation: Movement of fluid in the three semicircular canals tells the brain about the position and movement of the head; the cochlea is for hearing.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: After a heavy meal rich in starch, blood glucose is brought back to normal by insulin, which
questions.A: converts glycogen in the liver back into glucose
questions.B: stops the absorption of glucose from the ileum
questions.C: increases the breakdown of fats into fatty acids
questions.D: promotes the change of glucose to glycogen in the liver and muscles
questions.explanation: Insulin from the islets of Langerhans lowers blood glucose; glucagon does the opposite when glucose is low.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A frightened person has a pounding heart, dilated pupils and raised blood sugar. These changes are caused by
questions.explanation: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands prepares the body for 'fight or flight' in an emergency.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A swelling at the front of the neck (goitre) is usually caused by a shortage of iodine, because iodine is needed to make
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland enlarges as it tries to make enough thyroxine, the hormone that controls the metabolic rate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The pituitary is called the master gland because it
questions.A: is the largest endocrine gland in the body
questions.B: lies in the neck just below the larynx
questions.D: secretes hormones that control other endocrine glands
questions.explanation: Pituitary hormones regulate the thyroid, adrenal cortex, ovaries and testes, besides producing growth hormone and ADH.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: On a hot day the skin helps to cool the body by
questions.A: constricting the blood vessels and stopping sweat
questions.B: dilating the surface blood vessels and producing sweat that evaporates
questions.explanation: Vasodilation brings warm blood to the surface to lose heat, and evaporation of sweat takes latent heat from the skin.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The root of a seedling laid horizontally curves downwards after a day. This response is
questions.explanation: Roots grow towards the pull of gravity (positive geotropism); shoots grow away from it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk, the lizard is
questions.explanation: The grasshopper eats the producer (primary consumer); the lizard eats the grasshopper (secondary); the hawk is the tertiary consumer.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk, the least energy is available to the
questions.explanation: Only about 10 per cent of the energy at one level passes to the next, so the top consumer receives the least.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In a grassland, the dry mass of the grass is far greater than that of the antelopes feeding on it, which in turn is greater than that of the lions. A pyramid drawn from these masses is called a pyramid of
questions.explanation: A pyramid of biomass compares the dry mass of living material at each trophic level; a pyramid of numbers counts individuals and a pyramid of energy shows energy flow.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The instrument used to measure the relative humidity of the air in a habitat is the
questions.explanation: A wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer measures humidity; the anemometer measures wind speed and the rain gauge rainfall.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The turbidity (cloudiness) of a pond is measured with a
questions.explanation: The depth at which the black-and-white Secchi disc disappears from view indicates how turbid the water is.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Farmers plant cowpea or groundnut on a field to restore its fertility because these legumes
questions.A: need very little water and no fertiliser
questions.B: carry nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules
questions.C: produce large leaves that shade out weeds
questions.D: prevent all weeds from growing on the field
questions.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria in the nodules convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant, and later the soil, can use.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter are important in the nitrogen cycle because they
questions.A: convert nitrates in the soil back to nitrogen gas
questions.B: convert ammonium compounds to nitrites and then to nitrates
questions.C: fix nitrogen gas inside the root nodules of legumes
questions.D: break down proteins in dead matter into amino acids
questions.explanation: These nitrifying bacteria produce nitrates, the form of nitrogen plants absorb best; denitrifying bacteria do the reverse.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A lichen is an association between an alga and a fungus in which the alga makes food by photosynthesis and the fungus supplies water and anchorage. This relationship is
questions.explanation: Both partners benefit; lichens are also pioneer organisms on bare rock in primary succession.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The remora fish attaches itself to a shark and feeds on scraps from the shark's meals without harming it. This is an example of
questions.explanation: One partner benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed: commensalism.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The size of a population of lizards on an island would decrease as a result of an increase in
questions.explanation: Births and immigration add individuals; deaths and emigration remove them.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: An abandoned farm is first colonised by grasses, then shrubs, and after many years by forest trees. This sequence of changes is called
questions.explanation: Each community alters the habitat so that another can replace it, until a stable climax community (the forest) is reached.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A vegetation zone with tall grasses, scattered fire-resistant trees and distinct wet and dry seasons is
questions.explanation: The Guinea and Sudan savannas of Nigeria have these features; rainforest has continuous tall trees and mangroves grow in salt water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Mangrove trees of the Niger Delta have breathing roots (pneumatophores) that grow upwards out of the mud because
questions.A: the mud is waterlogged and poor in oxygen
questions.C: the roots absorb salt from the air
questions.D: they support the tree against the wind
questions.explanation: Pneumatophores take in oxygen for the submerged roots; prop (stilt) roots provide the support.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Competition between individuals of the same species is usually more intense than competition between different species because members of the same species
questions.explanation: Individuals of one species share the same food, space, mates and nesting sites, so every one of these is contested.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Desert plants such as cacti survive drought because they have
questions.A: broad thin leaves with a great many stomata
questions.B: succulent stems, leaves reduced to spines and sunken stomata
questions.C: shallow roots and stomata on both leaf surfaces
questions.D: large brightly coloured flowers all the year
questions.explanation: These features store water and reduce transpiration; long roots reach deep water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi are essential in an ecosystem because they
questions.A: produce the oxygen that animals breathe
questions.B: return nutrients from dead organisms to the soil and air
questions.C: eat living plants and keep them from spreading
questions.D: make the soil acidic so that weeds cannot grow
questions.explanation: By breaking down dead matter they release carbon dioxide, nitrogen compounds and minerals for producers to reuse.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Equal volumes of sandy, loamy and clay soils are placed in three funnels and the same volume of water is poured on each. The greatest volume of water drains through the sandy soil in ten minutes because sandy soil has
questions.B: large particles with large air spaces
questions.explanation: Large spaces between the coarse particles let water pass quickly; clay's tiny pores hold water back.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A farm remains waterlogged for days after rain. Its soil is most likely
questions.explanation: Clay particles are very small, so the pores are tiny and drainage is very poor.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Loamy soil is the best for growing most crops because it
questions.A: contains nothing but coarse sand, which drains very quickly
questions.B: has a balance of sand, clay and humus that drains well yet holds water
questions.C: stays wet all the year round, so crops never lack water
questions.D: contains no living organisms to attack crop roots
questions.explanation: Loam drains well yet holds enough water and nutrients, and is easy to work.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In a capillarity experiment, water rises highest, though slowly, in the tube containing
questions.explanation: The finer the particles, the narrower the capillary spaces and the greater the height to which water rises; in sand it rises fast but not far.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Humus improves a soil mainly because it
questions.A: makes the soil lighter in colour and cooler
questions.B: holds water and nutrients and improves soil structure
questions.C: kills the bacteria that live in the soil
questions.D: increases drainage in clay soils only
questions.explanation: Decayed organic matter binds particles into crumbs, retains moisture, supplies nutrients and darkens the soil so it warms faster.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Earthworms improve the fertility of soil by
questions.A: eating the roots of weeds so that crops grow better
questions.B: burrowing, which aerates the soil, and producing casts rich in nutrients
questions.C: carrying sand up to the surface to improve drainage
questions.D: removing dead leaves and humus from the surface
questions.explanation: Their tunnels admit air and water, and their casts and dead bodies add organic matter.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Heavy rain on a sandy farm carries dissolved nutrients down beyond the reach of crop roots. This loss is called
questions.explanation: Leaching removes soluble minerals such as nitrates; erosion removes the soil itself.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Which farming practice best restores nitrogen to a soil that has been cropped for several years?
questions.A: burning the stubble at the end of every season
questions.B: rotating cereals with legumes and adding manure
questions.C: planting maize continuously on the same field
questions.D: removing all crop residues after harvest
questions.explanation: Legumes fix nitrogen and manure adds organic nitrogen; continuous cropping and burning deplete it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: On a sloping farm, erosion by running water is best reduced by
questions.A: ploughing straight up and down the slope
questions.B: making ridges along the contours and planting cover crops
questions.C: removing all vegetation from the slope
questions.D: burning the grass before the rains begin
questions.explanation: Contour ridges slow the run-off and cover crops shield the soil from raindrops and bind it with roots.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Fertiliser washed from farms into a lake causes fish to die some weeks later because
questions.A: the fertiliser poisons the fish as soon as it reaches them
questions.B: algae multiply, then die and decay, using up the dissolved oxygen
questions.C: the water becomes too cold for the fish to breed
questions.D: the fish eat the fertiliser and cannot digest it
questions.explanation: This is eutrophication: the nutrient-rich water produces an algal bloom whose decomposition by bacteria removes oxygen.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Acid rain, which damages buildings and forests, is produced mainly by
questions.A: carbon dioxide from the respiration of animals
questions.B: sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen from burning fuels
questions.C: oxygen released by green plants in photosynthesis
questions.D: methane released by cattle and rice fields
questions.explanation: These gases dissolve in rain to form sulphuric and nitric acids.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) released from old refrigerators are harmful because they
questions.A: dissolve in rain water and make the rain acidic
questions.B: destroy the ozone layer, so more ultraviolet light reaches the earth
questions.C: poison the fish in rivers and lakes near cities
questions.D: block the sunlight that crops need to grow
questions.explanation: More ultraviolet light increases skin cancer and eye damage and harms crops and plankton.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The gas that contributes most to global warming because of its release from burning fossil fuels is
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide traps heat radiated from the earth (the greenhouse effect); methane and CFCs also contribute.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Discarded polythene bags are a lasting problem in Nigerian cities because they
questions.A: dissolve in rain water and poison the wells
questions.B: are non-biodegradable and block drains, causing floods
questions.C: attract earthworms and rats to the streets
questions.D: decay within a week and give off bad smells
questions.explanation: Micro-organisms cannot break polythene down, so it persists for many years.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Overgrazing by cattle in the northern savanna leads to desertification because
questions.A: cattle add so much manure that the soil becomes too rich
questions.B: removal of the grass cover exposes the soil to wind and water erosion
questions.C: cattle drink all the water in the rivers and wells
questions.D: grass grows back faster than the cattle can eat it
questions.explanation: Bare, trampled soil dries out, loses its top layer and can no longer support vegetation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: An outbreak of cholera in a village is most likely to follow the
questions.A: eating of unripe fruit from the farms
questions.B: contamination of the drinking water by sewage
questions.D: inhaling of dust during the harmattan
questions.explanation: Cholera and typhoid are water-borne diseases spread by faecal contamination of water and food; houseflies also carry the germs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The vector of sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis) in humans and cattle is the
questions.explanation: Tsetse flies (Glossina) transmit Trypanosoma; Anopheles carries malaria and blackflies carry river blindness.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Which of the following measures would best reduce the spread of malaria in a community?
questions.A: boiling all drinking water and washing hands before meals
questions.B: clearing stagnant water where mosquitoes breed and using treated nets
questions.C: vaccinating all the dogs and cats in the community
questions.D: spraying all the crops on the farms with fertiliser
questions.explanation: Malaria is transmitted only by the female Anopheles mosquito, so controlling the vector controls the disease.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Game reserves and national parks are established mainly to
questions.explanation: Protected areas prevent hunting and habitat destruction so that species do not become extinct.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In guinea pigs black coat (B) is dominant to white (b). A heterozygous black male is mated with a white female and 12 offspring are produced. The number of white offspring expected is
questions.explanation: Bb × bb gives 1 Bb (black) : 1 bb (white), so half of the 12 offspring, i.e. 6, are expected to be white.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In the cross Tt × Tt (tallness dominant), the genotypic ratio of the offspring is
questions.explanation: One TT : two Tt : one tt; the phenotypic ratio is 3 tall : 1 short.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: To find out whether a tall pea plant is TT or Tt, it should be crossed with
questions.explanation: A test cross with the recessive: if any short offspring appear the tall parent is Tt; if all are tall it is TT.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A pure-breeding tall pea plant was crossed with a pure-breeding short one and the F1 plants were allowed to self-pollinate. Out of 400 F2 plants, the number expected to be tall is
questions.explanation: F1 plants are all Tt; selfing gives 3 tall : 1 short, so three-quarters of 400, i.e. 300, are expected to be tall.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In cattle, a red bull mated with a white cow produces roan calves whose coats have both red and white hairs. This type of inheritance is
questions.explanation: In codominance both alleles are expressed fully in the heterozygote (red and white hairs side by side), unlike incomplete dominance where the heterozygote is intermediate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two pink-flowered four o'clock plants are crossed. The fraction of the offspring expected to be white is
questions.explanation: RW × RW gives RR (red), RW, RW (pink) and WW (white); one in four is white.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A man of blood group A and a woman of blood group B have a child of blood group O. The genotypes of the parents must be
questions.explanation: A group O child (ii) needs an i allele from each parent, so both parents are heterozygous.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two parents of blood group A have a child of blood group O. Which statement about the parents is correct?
questions.C: One parent must actually be group O
questions.explanation: A group O child (ii) receives one i allele from each parent, so both group A parents must be IAi; each therefore has a 1 in 4 chance of a group O child.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Both husband and wife have the sickle-cell trait (genotype AS). The probability that a child of theirs will have sickle-cell anaemia (SS) is
questions.explanation: AS × AS gives 1 AA : 2 AS : 1 SS, so each child has a one in four chance of being SS.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A couple in which one partner is AA and the other AS cannot have a child with sickle-cell anaemia because
questions.A: the S allele is never passed on to children
questions.B: every child receives an A allele from the AA parent
questions.C: the S allele is dominant over the A allele
questions.D: people of genotype AS are always sterile
questions.explanation: The children can only be AA or AS; both partners must carry S for an SS child to be possible.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The sex of a child is determined by the father because
questions.A: every egg carries a Y chromosome as well as an X
questions.B: sperms carry either an X or a Y chromosome while all eggs carry X
questions.C: the father has more chromosomes than the mother
questions.D: the Y chromosome is passed on only by the mother
questions.explanation: A Y-bearing sperm produces a boy (XY); an X-bearing sperm produces a girl (XX).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive condition. A haemophiliac man (XhY) marries a woman who is not a carrier (XHXH). Which of the following is correct about their children?
questions.A: all the daughters will be carriers but none of the sons will be affected
questions.B: all the sons will be haemophiliac and the daughters normal
questions.C: half the daughters and half the sons will be haemophiliac
questions.D: none of the children will receive the haemophilia allele
questions.explanation: Every daughter receives the father's Xh and the mother's XH, so all are carriers; sons receive the father's Y and a normal X from the mother, so none is affected.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In a dihybrid cross between two plants heterozygous for two independently inherited characters (RrYy × RrYy), the fraction of offspring showing both recessive characters is
questions.explanation: The 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio gives one double recessive (rryy) in sixteen.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Which of the following characters shows continuous variation in humans?
questions.explanation: Height varies gradually over a range because many genes and the environment influence it; the others fall into distinct classes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Mendel's first law (law of segregation) states that
questions.A: the characters of the two parents are blended in the offspring
questions.B: the two alleles of a pair separate so that each gamete carries only one
questions.C: characters acquired during life are passed to the offspring
questions.D: all the genes on a chromosome are always inherited together
questions.explanation: Each parent passes on one allele of each pair; the pair is restored at fertilisation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: In a disputed paternity case, a man of blood group O could not be the father of a child whose blood group is
questions.explanation: A group O father can give only the i allele, but an AB child must receive IA from one parent and IB from the other.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A sudden, heritable change in the genetic material of an organism is called
questions.explanation: Mutations may be caused by radiation or certain chemicals and are a source of new variation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Lamarck explained the long neck of the giraffe by suggesting that
questions.A: giraffes born with longer necks survived and reproduced more than others
questions.B: ancestral giraffes stretched their necks and passed the longer neck to their young
questions.C: the long neck arose by a sudden mutation in one generation
questions.D: giraffes were created with long necks and have never changed
questions.explanation: Lamarck's theory of use and disuse and the inheritance of acquired characters is not accepted today, because acquired changes are not inherited.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: According to Darwin's theory of natural selection,
questions.A: all the individuals of a species are exactly identical
questions.B: individuals with favourable variations survive and pass them to their offspring
questions.C: organisms change their bodies to suit their needs
questions.D: characters acquired during life are inherited by the young
questions.explanation: Variation, over-production, struggle for existence and survival of the fittest lead to gradual change in populations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: After clean-air laws reduced the soot on tree trunks in English cities, the pale form of the peppered moth became common again and the dark form declined. This shows that
questions.A: the moths changed colour to match the cleaner trees
questions.B: the direction of natural selection changes when the environment changes
questions.C: dark colour is caused by soot and not inherited
questions.D: pale moths reproduce faster than dark moths in all environments
questions.explanation: On clean, lichen-covered trunks the pale moths were now the better camouflaged ones, so birds ate more dark moths; selection favoured a different form when the environment changed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The flipper of a whale, the wing of a bat and the arm of a man have the same basic pentadactyl plan. Such structures are
questions.B: homologous and suggest descent from a common ancestor
questions.explanation: Homologous structures share origin and structure though they may differ in function; the wings of birds and insects are analogous.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The appendix and the coccyx in humans are described as vestigial organs because they
questions.A: are larger in humans than in any other mammals
questions.B: are reduced remnants of organs that worked in ancestral forms
questions.C: appeared only recently in the history of humans
questions.D: have no blood supply and no nerves of their own
questions.explanation: Vestigial organs are evidence of evolution: the coccyx is the remnant of a tail and the appendix of a larger caecum.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Archaeopteryx is regarded as evidence of evolution because its fossil shows
questions.A: a fish with four legs that could walk on dry land
questions.B: features of both reptiles (teeth, bony tail) and birds (feathers)
questions.C: the first flowering plant to appear on the earth
questions.D: a mammal with feathers instead of hair on its body
questions.explanation: It is a link between reptiles and birds, supporting the view that birds evolved from reptilian ancestors.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Darwin observed that finches on different Galapagos islands had beaks suited to different foods although they resembled one mainland species. This is an example of
questions.explanation: A single ancestral species gave rise to several species, each adapted to a different way of life.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Bacteria that survive a course of antibiotics multiply and produce resistant populations. This illustrates
questions.explanation: The drug kills susceptible bacteria; the few with resistance-conferring mutations survive and reproduce.
